You're auditing the new redesigned marketing-page templates at /opt/nxeon-staging (Next.js app, staging tree — do NOT touch /opt/nxeon prod tree, and do NOT run `npm run build` in EITHER tree, just read files). These live under `app/(marketing)/preview/*` — 17 preview routes for a page-template redesign (game landing pages, blog post, mods page, comparison, free-tier, AI-hosting, VPS, web-hosting, business-email, domains, nxcloud, location, app-hosting, tool, etc).

The owner just flagged a real bug: several of these pages are using a photo of the game "Rust" as a background/hero image even on pages that have nothing to do with Rust — they specifically called out this happening even on the **mods page** (`/preview/mods`), which is a general game-mods page, not Rust-specific. This smells like a placeholder image that got left in during the build-out and needs to be found everywhere it leaked.

Your job:
1. Find every image reference across all the preview template files and their shared components (`components/marketing/*template/`, `components/marketing/gamelanding/`, and any shared showcase/hero components they import). Look in `app/(marketing)/preview/**/*.tsx` and everything they import from `components/marketing/`.
2. For each image path/URL used (check `public/` for local images — likely under `public/games/`, `public/hero/`, or similar — and any external/CDN URLs), determine: (a) what the image actually shows (read the filename, check if there's a stored alt text, and if genuinely ambiguous, note it needs visual confirmation), (b) which page(s) it's used on, (c) whether that page's topic matches the image's actual subject.
3. Specifically confirm/deny the Rust-placeholder claim: grep for "rust" (case-insensitive) across the preview components and note every hit — filenames, import paths, variable names like `heroImage`, `bgImage`, `keyArt`, etc. Cross-reference against which page renders that component.
4. Produce a clear table/list: page → image file used → topic match (OK / MISMATCH: shows X but page is about Y). Flag every mismatch, not just the Rust ones — if any other game's art or a wrong stock photo shows up on an unrelated page, flag that too.
5. Do NOT fix anything yet — this is a diagnostic pass only. Just report findings.

Report back with the full mismatch table and a one-line root-cause guess for how the Rust image leaked across pages (e.g., "one shared component defaults to a single hardcoded heroImage prop and most callers never overrode it"). Keep the report scannable — a table, not prose paragraphs.
